newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers respond to tech industry concerns.
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers respond to tech industry concerns.

text.p: Technology companies are getting a sympathetic ear from some lawmakers in their efforts to curb what the firms describe as frivolous lawsuits.
Although this group, that includes software and biotech companies, won restrictions in 1995 affecting federal law, many of these lawsuits are now headed for state courts.
The Uniform Standards Coalition has been agressively lobbying Congress for its help.
Late last week, Representative Tom Campbell, a California Republican, introduced a measure that would ban private securities litigation altogether from moving to state courts.
But Campbell's bill is much broader and far reaching than what the industry wanted.
Instead, the coalition is supporting a bill due to be introduced Wednesday by California Democrat Rep. Anna Eshoo and Rep. Rick White, a Republican from Washington.

Eshoo and White's measure would curb only securities class actions rather than private actions from moving to state courts, industry sources said. That bill is also expected to be co-sponsored by Louisiana Republican Rep. Billy Tauzin.

"What we are looking for is a targeted approach," said Michael Timmeny, vice president for domestic policy for the American Electronics Association which is part of the coalition. "We think that the legislation which Rep. White and Rep. Eshoo will introduce is very targeted," Timmeny said.

Eshoo and White's bill will also contain a provision that would expressely remove any such securities class actions from state courts, while Campbell's bill would not include such specific language, industry sources say.

In 1995, Congress enacted legislation over President Clinton's veto, which was designed to reduce the amount of meritless cases in federal courts by, among other things, raising the qualifying standards.

The technology industry coalition claims that a small group of lawyers that specializes in securities class action suits has evaded the 1995 reforms by shifting cases to state courts, where the qualifying standards are lower.
Those opposed to the reforms include consumer groups, which have cautioned that the new standards leave investors with little legal recourse.
